analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to warn workers of layoffs and closures and to pay severance and continued health benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its April 1996 introduction it was referred to the House labor committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died with 20 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 100 or more employees to give workers, their union, local elected officials, and the Labor Department three months' written notice before a layoff, shutdown, or relocation. It would have required those employers to offer affected workers a choice between severance pay and rehiring preference at other company sites, keep paying the employer's share of health insurance premiums for a year, and make a good-faith offer to sell a closing plant to the community or its employees. It also would have directed the Labor Department to coordinate aid to displaced workers and study whether the community or employees could buy and keep the business running.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at workplaces with 100 or more employees who face a layoff, shutdown, or relocation would gain three months' written notice, a choice between severance pay (one week per year of service plus a bonus for every five years, with a three-week minimum) and permanent hiring preference at the employer's other workplaces, a year of continued employer-paid health and insurance premiums, and moving-cost help if transferred 40 miles or more [S2][S3]. Their unions, the towns where plants close, and the Labor Department would also receive notice and help studying employee- or community-owned buyouts [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing layoffs at large workplaces

how_it_helps.text: Gives workers three months' written warning of a planned layoff, shutdown, or relocation, including the reasons and the number of people affected — far longer than the 60 days then required under the federal WARN Act for much larger plants.

Requires a choice between severance pay (one week per year of service, plus a bonus week for every five years, with a three-week minimum) and permanent hiring preference with earned vacation, health, welfare, and pension benefits at the employer's other workplaces.
Keeps the employer paying its share of health and insurance premiums for a year after the layoff, or until the worker is rehired with benefits, so families do not lose coverage immediately.

Requires a good-faith offer to sell a closing or relocating plant, equipment, and inventory at fair market value to the community or to employee groups trying to form an employee-, community-, or jointly owned business, with Labor Department feasibility studies and technical assistance.
Backs the notice requirement with teeth: up to $1,000 per affected employee in civil penalties and back pay and lost benefits for workers when an employer fails to give notice.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 100 or more employees, who would bear the cost of advance notice, severance pay, a year of continued health insurance premiums, relocation reimbursements, the good-faith offer to sell closed plants, and civil penalties and back-pay liability for violations [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers closing or shrinking workplaces

drawbacks.text: The costs would fall hardest on employers closing plants precisely because they are struggling; severance for every year of service and a year of employer-paid health premiums could deepen a failing company's losses and push more jobs out of a community before the law's notice period even begins.
The bill exempts employers in bankruptcy and reductions caused by unforeseen events, so workers at companies that fail suddenly — often the most vulnerable — would get none of these protections.

The requirement to offer a closing plant for sale at fair market value could complicate and delay orderly shutdowns and relocations, and the $500 cap on relocation closing costs is small relative to the moving burden it addresses.
The 100-employee threshold leaves workers at smaller employers — where many layoffs happen — entirely outside the law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers at large workplaces facing closure, the protections were substantial: real advance warning, guaranteed severance or transfer rights, and a year of continued health coverage, backed by penalties. The honest trade-off is that the costs land on companies at the moment they are failing, which could speed up some closures, and the bankruptcy and unforeseen-event exemptions mean the workers most likely to be abandoned get the least. The 30-day health continuation and severance floors were modest by European standards, and the $500 relocation cap was low. On balance it was a meaningful worker-protection bill whose main weakness was cost placement rather than design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House labor committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended, and no vote was ever taken on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 30, 1996 and referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities the same day [S1][S5].
On May 17, 1996 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it remained with no hearings, markup, or floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].
All 20 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican sponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers facing plant closures or mass layoffs came out ahead, because the new notice, severance, health-coverage, and plant-sale obligations never took effect. Workers who lost jobs in the meantime had no additional protections under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers facing closures, who avoided new duties

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: The committee referred the bill to a subcommittee on May 17, 1996, and took no further action; no markup or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were House Democrats — and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the chamber's split was never tested.

industries.industry: Large employers (100+ employees) in manufacturing and other industries with plant closures
industries.note: The bill would have imposed notice, severance, health-continuation, and plant-sale obligations on employers of 100 or more workers at the very moment they shut or move a facility, plus civil penalties up to $1,000 per worker and back-pay liability for violations [S2][S3]. These employers had an interest in the bill never becoming law.

Unions and their members would have received advance notice and a role in bargaining over closures, and collective bargaining agreements would have prevailed over the statute where they conflict [S3].

Employee and community groups would have gained a good-faith right to buy closing plants at fair market value, with Labor Department feasibility studies and technical assistance, and collective bargaining agreements would carry over to any buyer [S3].
